doc.title: Ralph LaLama interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, May 23, 2010

title: Technology, communication and free downloads
summary: Technology reduces personal contact but helps communication; anyone can now make a CD, which lowers quality.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: How the music business changed: hype, youth and lost apprenticeship

blocks.x: Has the explosion in technology in the last ten years had an effect on what you do?

Not what I do but I think it has an effect on the scene. Yeah. Because that’s the way people are living and people, especially with the computers, I don’t feel, even the cell phones, I don’t feel that there’s so much personal contact. I remember when I walked down the street, “Hey man how you doin’?” Now it’s like you can’t even get their attention {mumbles}. And they’re driving, and stay in your lane, and when are you going to pick out the furniture? You know they’re hugging you. What do you want to propose? I mean I don’t know I just think that, I don’t know if that’s the technology you’re talking about but I think it’s the way of the world. But what I like about the technology is the

way you can communicate. Email, I could call Europe for free. Or I could email a thousand things at one time. And it’s be great. That’s great business. I love it. I really do, I love it. I think that’s the greatest thing. But like I have a lot of students, and their whole life is just doing this. And that really is absorbed. Because there’s so many things to absorb that you don’t absorb anything. And then the communication skills are — actually could you talk? What’s your name? Duh? What are you trying to tell me? Because their communication skills are down. They don’t interact. And I don’t think that’s good, we’re human beings, we’ve got to interact, we’ve got to have relationships, you know what I mean? Even in business. We’ve got to have relationships with people. Jazz business, lawyer business, doctor business, garbage can business, paint business, you know? It’s called relationships.
Is there less of an initiative these days to make recordings because of the way they get sent out and often times lifted for free.

Oh yeah. I don’t know if there’s less. I mean maybe you would think that way in philosophy but in reality I don’t think it’s less at all, I think it’s more, because everybody can do it. You know what I mean? But I don’t think it’s that — I don’t know what the word is — I don’t think it works out that well because of that, the download for free, you know you don’t make any money you know what I mean? And so I’m saying the reality doesn’t seem like it really has a deterrent on it. It seems like it’s more, because it’s easier to do.

Yeah, yeah. So like anybody can make a record, a CD, anybody. So to me and that brings down the quality too. You know what I mean? I have a CD out, I shouldn’t — I’m not saying you couldn’t for ten years, but right now you shouldn’t be worrying about that, you should be trying to make relationships. You know what I mean?
